title: Cost- and Org-Aware Design
summary: Designing with organizational constraints as first-class inputs — build vs buy, the operational burden a design creates, who ends up on call for it, and designing for the team you actually have.

slides.markdown:
At senior levels, "the best design" isn't purely a technical question — it's technical constraints plus organizational ones: what this costs to run, who operates it, whether the team has the skills and time to do it well. Ignoring those inputs doesn't make a design more correct, it just makes it wrong in a way that shows up months later as an operational mess.

This topic is the cost/ownership/team-fit lens applied to any single design decision — not the cross-team, org-chart-level trade-offs that come up at staff/principal scope, which are covered elsewhere.

slides.sectionTitle: Build vs buy: the real cost of "we could build that ourselves"
slides.markdown:
"We could build that ourselves" is almost always true and almost always the wrong frame — the real question isn't *can we*, it's *should we*, and that depends on comparing total cost, not just the interesting part of the work. Building a message queue, a feature-flag system, or an auth layer is a fun, scoped engineering problem for the first three months; then it needs on-call, security patches, and feature parity with the ecosystem forever after.

Buying (a managed service, an established open-source tool, a vendor) usually costs more upfront and less over time, because the maintenance burden shifts to someone whose full-time job it is. Build makes sense when the thing you'd build is your actual differentiator — where owning the internals is the competitive advantage — not when it's undifferentiated infrastructure every company needs.

Interview signal: don't answer build-vs-buy with a flat preference — name what's actually being compared: the buy option's ongoing cost and lock-in risk against the build option's ongoing maintenance burden and opportunity cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Operational burden as a design cost, not an implementation detail
slides.markdown:
**Operational burden** is the ongoing human cost of keeping a design running: pages, upgrades, capacity planning, incident response, the on-call rotation it adds load to. It's easy to leave out of a design comparison because it doesn't show up until after launch — the doc that only compares build cost and latency numbers is missing the cost that actually accrues for years.

A design choice that looks technically superior (better throughput, cleaner abstraction) can be the wrong choice once you price in that it needs a specialized skill set to operate, or that it pages the team twice as often as the boring alternative. That's not a hypothetical trade-off — it's a real, recurring cost that should be estimated and stated in the doc, not discovered the first time someone gets paged at 3am.

A useful habit: for any design with meaningful operational surface, write one sentence naming what it'll page for and roughly how often, before it ships — not as a guess after the fact.

slides.sectionTitle: Who's on call for this: designing with the owning team's reality in mind
slides.markdown:
Every design decision implicitly names an owner — the team that gets paged when it breaks. Making that explicit, and asking whether *that specific team* can actually operate the thing, changes designs in ways a purely technical review won't.

A design that assumes deep Kafka expertise is a fine choice for a team that already runs Kafka at scale, and a real liability for a team of three that's never operated a distributed log — the failure won't show up in code review, it'll show up as a 2am page nobody on that team knows how to diagnose. "Who's on call for this" isn't a bureaucratic question — it's asking whether the design matches the operational reality of the specific humans who'll carry it.

When the answer is uncomfortable — the best technical choice would land on a team that can't support it — that's a real constraint on the design, not something to route around by hoping training happens later.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: total cost of ownership across build, run, and maintain
slides.markdown:
![Total cost of ownership over three years: build in-house grows each year while buy stays flat after a higher start](assets/tco-comparison.svg)

**Total cost of ownership** is build cost plus run cost plus maintain cost, summed over the design's realistic lifetime — not just the number in the initial proposal. Comparing only build cost is why "build it ourselves" often looks like the cheap option on day one and the expensive one three years in.

The practical habit: whenever a design comparison shows only an upfront number, ask for the same comparison extended out 2-3 years, including the team-time cost of running and maintaining each option.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing for the team you have: skills, headcount, and time horizon as constraints
slides.markdown:
The team's current skills, headcount, and realistic time horizon are as much a design constraint as latency or throughput requirements — treating them as separate from "the real design" is how a team ends up owning something it can't actually run well.

A five-person team with no distributed-systems background and a deadline in six weeks has a different correct answer than a twenty-person platform team with a year of runway, even for the identical problem. Designing for the team you wish you had, rather than the one you have, produces a design that's correct on a whiteboard and painful in production.

This isn't lowering the bar — it's the same discipline as capacity estimation applied to the team itself: state the real constraint, then design within it, rather than assuming it away.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: the "correct" design vs the design this team can actually operate
slides.markdown:
| | The "correct" design | The design this team can operate |
|---|---|---|
| Optimizes for | Best technical fit for the stated problem in isolation | Best outcome given this team's actual skills, headcount, and time |
| Common example | A custom distributed cache tuned exactly to the access pattern | A well-known managed cache service, slightly less optimal on paper |
| Risk if chosen wrong | Elegant on a whiteboard, unsupportable in production, becomes a liability the team can't safely change | Slightly higher steady-state cost, but the team can actually debug, extend, and operate it |
| Interview framing | "Here's the theoretically best architecture" | "Here's the best architecture given these constraints, and here's what I'd revisit if the team grows" |

**How to decide:** state both — the theoretically ideal design and the one that fits the team — explicitly, and pick the latter unless the gap between them is small enough that the team can grow into it before it matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: choosing the interesting technology over the boring one that fits
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This new database/framework is more interesting and technically superior, so it's the right choice."

**Why it's wrong:** "more interesting" and "the right fit for this team and problem" are unrelated properties, and conflating them is a well-documented failure pattern — the team adopts a system nobody has operated before, hits an undocumented failure mode at 2am, and burns weeks relearning lessons the boring, well-understood alternative already had answers for. The excitement of the technology doesn't offset the real cost of the team's unfamiliarity with it.

**Correct model:** treat "boring and well-understood by this team" as a real point in a technology's favor, not a lack of ambition — reserve the interesting, unproven choice for the parts of the system where the differentiation it buys you is actually worth the operational unknowns.

"Building it ourselves is cheaper long-term" needs a number attached before it's a real argument. Say a managed queue service costs $2,000/month at your scale, versus self-hosting the equivalent on 3 nodes at $300/month in infrastructure — a naive comparison says build wins by $1,700/month.

But add the cost the naive version skips: one engineer spending even 20% of their time (roughly $30,000/year fully loaded, so ~$500/month) on patching, scaling, and on-call for that self-hosted queue already erases most of the saving — and that's before counting the incident where nobody on the team has operated a queue cluster before and a 2am outage takes four hours instead of one.

The habit to bring into an interview isn't a precise number — it's showing the calculation includes operational headcount cost, not just the infrastructure line item, which is where "obviously cheaper to build" arguments usually go wrong.
